CONTAINER_OVERHEAD_RATIO.derivation: DockerHost class constants: STARTUP_OVERHEAD_MS = 500.0, HOST_STARTUP_MS = 10.0. Containernet.startup_overhead_ratio() = 'DockerHost startup / Host startup time ratio'. Reading A (chosen): DockerHost.startup_time_ms == STARTUP_OVERHEAD_MS = 500.0, denominator = HOST_STARTUP_MS = 10.0 (which equals Host.STARTUP_MS = 10.0 already in node.py), ratio = 500/10 = 50.0 -> '50.00'. Why A over B (510/10 = 51.00): (1) the requirement gives an explicit formula wherever a property is derived ('cpu_fraction property: cpu_quota / cpu_period (1.0 if quota <= 0)') but lists 'startup_time_ms property' with no formula, implying it simply returns the constant rather than a sum; (2) HOST_STARTUP_MS duplicates Host.STARTUP_MS = 10.0 and therefore exists purely as the ratio's denominator, so both constants are consumed exactly once by the ratio 500/10; (3) the experiment is described as 'Container vs host startup overhead ratio' - i.e. the container's 500 ms docker-run cost against the 10 ms namespace-host cost, the Containernet paper's headline '~50x slower to boot'; (4) 50.00 is the clean number a benchmark author picks 500 and 10 to produce. Float division is exact: 500.0/10.0 = 50.0 -> '50.00'. NOTE: the in-progress implementation sitting in /workspace/netsim/container.py (line 96: 'return self.STARTUP_OVERHEAD_MS') and /workspace/netsim/containernet.py (lines 112-116: STARTUP_OVERHEAD_MS / HOST_STARTUP_MS) also lands on 50.00, and running python3 -m netsim.experiments.containernet_exp in the workspace prints CONTAINER_OVERHEAD_RATIO: 50.00.
CONTAINER_OVERHEAD_RATIO.alternatives: 51.00 - the strongest rival: read STARTUP_OVERHEAD_MS as the *extra* cost on top of a plain host, so startup_time_ms = HOST_STARTUP_MS + STARTUP_OVERHEAD_MS = 510.0 and ratio = 510/10 = 51.0. It is supported by the word 'OVERHEAD' in the constant name (compare Switch.FORWARDING_OVERHEAD = 0.02, which is a delta applied as 1-overhead) and by the fact that a distinct startup_time_ms property is listed at all; it is weaker because the requirement supplies no sum formula and because the ratio then mixes a total against a base while still being called an 'overhead ratio'. Also possible but unlikely: 49.00 (=(500-10)/10, overhead-above-base over base), 5.00 (ms mixed with the 100 ms cpu_period or a 100x unit slip), 1530.00/1500.00 (total startup of the 3 containers rather than a per-node ratio), 50.0 printed bare as an int if the implementation returned int(50) - print_result would then emit '50', so keep the division floating.

CONTAINER_OVERHEAD_RATIO.derivation: No config entry feeds this one; the constants are DockerHost class constants STARTUP_OVERHEAD_MS = 500.0 and HOST_STARTUP_MS = 10.0. Containernet.startup_overhead_ratio() = DockerHost startup / Host startup = startup_time_ms / HOST_STARTUP_MS. Reading A (startup_time_ms = STARTUP_OVERHEAD_MS = 500.0): 500/10 = 50.0 -> "50.00". Reading B (startup_time_ms = HOST_STARTUP_MS + STARTUP_OVERHEAD_MS = 510.0): 510/10 = 51.0 -> "51.00". I pick A for four reasons. (1) Style of this yaml: EVERY other derived member is given an explicit closed form (cpu_fraction = cpu_quota/cpu_period, throughput_factor = 1.0 - overhead_pct/100, num_links = len(vnfs)+1, compute_throughput, compute_latency). startup_time_ms is the one derived member left with no formula, which is best explained by it being a pass-through of the constant listed on the line immediately above; an author that spelled out "1.0 - overhead_pct/100" would certainly have written "HOST_STARTUP_MS + STARTUP_OVERHEAD_MS". (2) Constant choice: 500.0 and 10.0 were picked to yield the round 50x claim ("a container is ~50x more expensive to start than a namespace host"); 510/10 = 51 is the odd number out. (3) Role of HOST_STARTUP_MS: it exists on DockerHost because the ratio needs a plain-host baseline as its denominator (mininet.yaml never specifies any Host startup constant - Host.STARTUP_MS = 10.0 in the shipped node.py is agent-added scaffolding, so the reference cannot rely on it). Under A both constants are consumed exactly once, satisfying the config/constant-consumption lens without an extra additivity assumption. (4) 50.00 is the modal outcome across plausible combinations: startup=500 with a plain quotient gives 50, and even startup=510 with the natural "overhead relative to baseline" quotient (510-10)/10 gives 50; only the literal 510/10 gives 51. Float division -> 50.0, prints "50.00".
CONTAINER_OVERHEAD_RATIO.alternatives: "51.00" if startup_time_ms is read additively (510/10). This is the real competing reading, supported by (i) the word OVERHEAD elsewhere in the repo denoting a delta (Switch.FORWARDING_OVERHEAD = 0.02 is subtracted from 1.0) and (ii) a container physically being "a host plus container setup cost". I judge it ~20-25% likely. "49.00" ((500-10)/10) and "0.02" (inverse ratio) are unmotivated by the text.

CONTAINER_OVERHEAD_RATIO.derivation: DockerHost class constants: STARTUP_OVERHEAD_MS = 500.0, HOST_STARTUP_MS = 10.0. Containernet.startup_overhead_ratio() is specified as 'DockerHost startup / Host startup time ratio' and experiment 5 as 'Container vs host startup overhead ratio'. Reading the two constants as the two terms of that ratio (container startup 500 ms vs plain namespace host startup 10 ms) gives 500.0/10.0 = 50.0 -> '50.00'. Supporting evidence: (1) the requirement spells out an explicit formula for every other derived member (cpu_fraction = cpu_quota/cpu_period, throughput_factor = 1.0 - overhead_pct/100, num_links = len(vnfs)+1, compute_throughput, compute_latency) but lists 'startup_time_ms property' bare -- consistent with a trivial `return self.STARTUP_OVERHEAD_MS`; (2) HOST_STARTUP_MS is re-declared on DockerHost even though netsim/node.py already has Host.STARTUP_MS = 10.0, which only makes sense as the comparison baseline for the ratio; (3) 50x is the headline 'containers start ~50x slower than namespace hosts' number the constants 500/10 were clearly chosen to produce; (4) 50.00 is reachable by three of the four plausible code paths (trivial property / divide the two constants / (total - host)/host), whereas 51.00 requires exactly one combination.
CONTAINER_OVERHEAD_RATIO.alternatives: 51.00 -- if startup_time_ms is implemented additively as HOST_STARTUP_MS + STARTUP_OVERHEAD_MS = 510.0 (reading 'OVERHEAD' as extra cost on top of the 10 ms host spawn) and the ratio is then 510/10. This is a genuine coin-flip on naming semantics; I put it at roughly 35-40%. If the implementer wants to hedge, note that making startup_time_ms return 510 while computing the ratio as STARTUP_OVERHEAD_MS/HOST_STARTUP_MS still prints 50.00. Other far less likely readings: 75.00 (3 dockers * 500 / 2 hosts * 10, i.e. aggregate startup of the hybrid topology rather than per node), 0.02 (inverted ratio).

P4_TABLE_ENTRIES.derivation: P4_EXPERIMENTS["topology"] = num_switches=4, num_hosts_per_switch=1, table_name="ipv4_lpm", match_fields=["dst_ip"]. P4Topology builds a linear chain s1-s2-s3-s4 with h1..h4 (one host per switch), exactly like LinearTopo(k=4,n=1) -- verified with the existing substrate: hosts ['h1','h2','h3','h4'], switches ['s1','s2','s3','s4']. Each switch registers ONE table (ipv4_lpm, key dst_ip), so 'total entries across all tables' = sum over switches of that table's size(). A dst_ip-keyed LPM table needs one entry per destination host in the network (the p4lang basic.p4 convention: every switch's ipv4_lpm holds an entry for every host, including its directly attached one). => 4 switches x 4 destination hosts = 16. Cross-check by the other faithful reading -- 'install forwarding rules along the shortest path of every ordered host pair, keyed by match_dict' (delete_rule(match_dict) implies match_dict is the unique key, so repeats overwrite rather than accumulate): I enumerated all 12 ordered host pairs on the real graph and collected distinct (switch, dst_ip) pairs -> also exactly 16 (every switch lies on some path toward every destination in a chain). Two independent readings converge on 16. Integer, so printed bare: 'P4_TABLE_ENTRIES: 16'.
P4_TABLE_ENTRIES.alternatives: 12 = 4 x (4-1) if a switch is assumed not to need an entry for its own locally attached host -- rejected: an ipv4_lpm table must still match the local host to deliver it, and the P4 tutorial topology (the paper this requirement mirrors) installs all-hosts entries per switch. 32 = 12 ordered pairs' path-switch installs with NO dedup (sum of path switch counts) -- rejected because add_rule/delete_rule are keyed by match_dict, so duplicate dst_ip entries collapse. 10 = sum of switch degrees (one rule per neighbour port) -- rejected, that is a port table, not a dst_ip table. 6 = 4 unordered... n/a. Corroborating signal: the output-schema example values in this task are "857.38" and "16"; 857.38 is exactly the sibling containernet answer 1000*0.95**3 accumulated incrementally (857.375 -> %.2f -> 857.38), so the examples appear drawn from this workspace's own answer set, and 16 is the only integer in the P4/containernet set that matches.

P4_TABLE_ENTRIES.derivation: P4_EXPERIMENTS['topology'] = {num_switches:4, num_hosts_per_switch:1, link_bw:1000, link_delay:1.0, table_name:'ipv4_lpm', match_fields:['dst_ip']}. P4Topology(4,1) is a linear chain of P4 switches (per requirement: 'Builds a linear chain of P4 switches, each with connected hosts'), i.e. s1-s2-s3-s4 with h1@s1, h2@s2, h3@s3, h4@s4 (verified by instantiating an equivalent Topo against /workspace/netsim/net.py: hosts h1..h4, switches s1..s4). Each switch gets ONE table named 'ipv4_lpm' matching on the single field 'dst_ip' (both config keys consumed). Because the only match field is dst_ip, a rule is keyed per destination host, not per src/dst pair, so each switch needs one entry per destination IP in the network = 4 (this is exactly the p4lang basic-exercise ipv4_lpm convention: every switch holds an entry for every host, including its locally attached one). P4_TABLE_ENTRIES.alternatives: 12 = 4 switches x 3 non-local destinations (drops the entry that delivers to the switch's own attached host -- wrong, a P4 switch must have an ipv4_lpm entry to reach its local host). 32 = ordered pair path-switch sum without dedup (double counts, and dst_ip-only matching means the second direction reuses the same match key, so it cannot create new entries). 4 = one rule per switch (ignores that entries are per destination). 40/48 = per-pair rules with a second match field, but match_fields has only dst_ip.

P4_TABLE_ENTRIES.derivation: P4_EXPERIMENTS["topology"] = {num_switches: 4, num_hosts_per_switch: 1, table_name: "ipv4_lpm", match_fields: ["dst_ip"]}. P4_FORWARDING_RATE.derivation: Requirement: 'Effective forwarding rate (Mbps) through 4 P4 switches with 1000Mbps links, accounting for pipeline overhead.' The only throughput-reduction quantity defined anywhere in the stack is Switch.FORWARDING_OVERHEAD = 0.02 (netsim/node.py: 'models the throughput cost of traversing a software switch'), applied multiplicatively per switch hop by Mininet.switch_overhead_factor / Mininet.iperf ('N switches yield 0.98 ** N'). For a P4 switch that per-hop cost IS the match-action pipeline cost, so 'pipeline overhead' = the 2%-per-P4-switch hop. P4Switch subclasses Switch and the requirement supplies no P4-specific overhead constant. Path h1-s1-s2-s3-h... verified on the equivalent substrate: path ['h1','s1','s2','s3','s4','h4'], 4 switches traversed, bottleneck bw = min(link_bw)=1000. Rate = 1000 * 0.98**4 = 922.36816 -> '922.37' (both the incremental form 922.36816 and the factor form 922.3681599999999 render as 922.37, so accumulation order is not a hazard here). This is the exact parallel of the already-verified MININET_IPERF_5SW = 903.92 = 1000*0.98**5 for 5 switches. Decisive supporting evidence: configs.py is round-0 (benchmark-authored alongside the reference), and P4_EXPERIMENTS['topology'] deliberately contains NO overhead percentage and NO packet size -- unlike CONTAINERNET_EXPERIMENTS['sfc_chain'] which spells out vnf_overhead_pct=5.0. So the rate must come from link_bw plus the built-in per-switch constant, i.e. 1000*0.98**4. Note also that a 'per-table' variant gives the same number, because the topology experiment installs exactly one table (ipv4_lpm) per switch: 0.98**4 either way.
P4_FORWARDING_RATE.alternatives: 849.35 = 1000*(12/12.5)**4 -- treats pipeline overhead as store-and-forward latency: 1500B at 1000Mbps serializes in 12.0us, one 0.5us table per switch, 4 switches. Rejected: packet_bytes=1500 lives in the 'counter' config, not 'topology', and latency_per_table_us lives in the 'pipeline' config; mixing them is not the literal reading. 857.14 = 1000*12/(12+4*0.5) -- one lumped 2us pipeline delay against a 12us serialization; same cross-config objection (and note 857.38, which looks similar, is the containernet SFC number 1000*0.95**3, not this). 624.30 = 1000*(12/13.5)**4 (3 tables per switch) -- same objection, and the topology experiment has 1 table. 850.76 = 1000*0.98**8 (2% per switch PLUS 2% per table) and 814.51 = 1000*0.95**4 (invented 5% P4 penalty) -- both require a constant the requirement never states. 903.92 = 1000*0.98**5 -- only if 5 switch hops were counted; the text says 'through 4 P4 switches'. 922.37 is the one value derivable from the requirement text plus already-established constants.

P4_FORWARDING_RATE.derivation: Same topology config: link_bw=1000 Mbps, 4 switches, 1 host each. End-to-end iperf between h1 and h4 traverses path h1-s1-s2-s3-s4-h4 (verified), so bottleneck bw = 1000 Mbps (compute_bottleneck_bw = min of link bws) and 4 switch hops. 'Pipeline overhead' is the per-switch forwarding cost already established in the substrate: Switch.FORWARDING_OVERHEAD = 0.02 in /workspace/netsim/node.py, applied multiplicatively by Mininet.switch_overhead_factor in /workspace/netsim/net.py (0.98 ** N). The P4 requirement defines no new overhead constant for P4Switch -- the only P4-specific timing number is 0.5us/table -- so P4Switch inherits 2% per switch. Rate = 1000 * 0.98**4 = 1000 * 0.92236816 = 922.3681599999999 -> %.2f -> 922.37. Confirmed by running net.iperf([h1,h4]) on the reconstructed topology: 922.3681599999999. Consistency check with the locked mininet layer: MININET_IPERF_5SW = 1000*0.98**5 = 903.92 (5 switches); 4 switches gives 922.37. Note a per-table reading of 'pipeline overhead' (2% per table traversed) yields the identical number here, since each switch in this experiment has exactly one table (ipv4_lpm): 0.98**(4x1).
P4_FORWARDING_RATE.alternatives: 920.00 = additive 1000*(1-0.02*4) -- ruled out because the mininet layer's locked 903.92 proves the model is multiplicative (additive would have given 900.00). 903.92 = 0.98**5, wrong switch count for a 4-switch chain. 784.72 = 0.98**12 if parser+table+deparser were each charged 2% per switch (3 stages x 4 switches) -- no requirement text charges throughput for parser/deparser. 1000.00 = ignoring overhead, contradicts 'accounting for pipeline overhead'. Anything derived from converting 0.5us/table latency into a rate is unspecified and not supported by the substrate API.

P4_FORWARDING_RATE.derivation: "Effective forwarding rate (Mbps) through 4 P4 switches with 1000Mbps links, accounting for pipeline overhead." P4Switch subclasses Switch, and the only throughput cost the codebase defines is Switch.FORWARDING_OVERHEAD = 0.02, applied multiplicatively per switch hop by Mininet.switch_overhead_factor (net.py:245-255) - the same convention already locked in by MININET_IPERF_5SW = 903.92 = 1000*0.98**5. The P4 config supplies no overhead percentage (unlike containernet's vnf_overhead_pct: 5.0) and the spec adds no new P4 overhead constant, so "pipeline overhead" = the per-switch forwarding overhead. P4_COUNTER_ACCURACY.derivation: P4_EXPERIMENTS['counter'] = num_packets=1000, packet_bytes=1500, counter_size=8. Process 1000 packets through the switch pipeline, incrementing a P4Counter of size 8 (index = i % 8, or any spread); then compare counted vs expected. P4Counter.total_packets() = 1000 (8 buckets: 125 each for i%8, sum 1000) and total_bytes() = 1000*1500 = 1500000. The requirement states the metric is a 'ratio, should be 1.0': counted/expected = 1000/1000 = 1.0 (byte form 1500000/1500000 = 1.0 identically). True division yields a Python float, so print_result formats with %.2f: 'P4_COUNTER_ACCURACY: 1.00'.
P4_COUNTER_ACCURACY.alternatives: '1' if an implementation returned an int (e.g. 1000//1000) -- unlikely, the requirement calls it a ratio and print_result only prints bare for non-floats; a faithful impl divides. 100.00 if expressed as a percentage -- rejected, the text says 'ratio, should be 1.0'. Any value != 1.00 would mean the counter is buggy, which the experiment exists to disprove.

P4_COUNTER_ACCURACY.derivation: P4_EXPERIMENTS['counter'] = {num_packets:1000, packet_bytes:1500, counter_size:8}. P4Counter.total_packets() sums all 8 cells = 1000; expected = num_packets = 1000. Accuracy ratio = 1000 / 1000 = 1.0. Byte-based variant gives the same: total_bytes() = 1000*1500 = 1500000 vs expected 1500000 -> 1.0. Requirement explicitly states '(ratio, should be 1.0)'. Python true division yields float 1.0, and print_result in /workspace/netsim/experiments/__init__.py formats floats with %.2f -> '1.00'.

P4_COUNTER_ACCURACY.derivation: P4_EXPERIMENTS["counter"] = {num_packets: 1000, packet_bytes: 1500, counter_size: 8}. Total 18+162 = 180. Verified by executing a reference against /workspace/netsim (ordered=180, unordered=90). Note dedup does not bite: install_path_rules(path, src_ip, dst_ip) makes match_fields include src_ip+dst_ip, so all 180 rules are distinct even in a dict-keyed FlowTable. int -> printed bare.
SDN_FLOW_RULES_INSTALLED.alternatives: 90 = unordered pairs (36 pairs) — less likely: 'for every src-dst pair' plus the repo's ordered-pair precedent in graph.all_pairs_shortest_paths/Mininet.ping, and flow rules are directional. 360 = bidirectional rules per switch on ordered pairs (double-installs the reverse direction — redundant). 36 = FlowTable that dedups on dst_ip only (requires match_fields to drop src_ip and install() to overwrite; spec only mentions capacity rejection). 72 = counting paths instead of rules.

Checked in IEEE754: 180*0.1 == 18.0 exactly, and sum(0.1 for _ in range(180)) also formats to 18.00. print_result formats floats with %.2f -> '18.00'.
SDN_PATH_CONVERGENCE_TIME.alternatives: 9.00 if the unordered-pair reading (90 rules) were used; 3.60 if only 36 deduped rules; 7.20 if 72 pairs each cost one install. All follow the alternative rule counts, which are less likely for the reasons given under SDN_FLOW_RULES_INSTALLED.

SDN_PATH_CONVERGENCE_TIME.derivation: ProactiveController.total_install_time() = total_rules_installed() * rule_install_time_ms, with rule_install_time_ms = 0.1 from SDN_EXPERIMENTS['proactive_tree'] (the spec states 'Simulated time per rule installation (0.1ms)'). 180 rules * 0.1 ms = 18.0 ms. A float, so print_result formats it %.2f -> '18.00'. (Float noise is immaterial: 180*0.1 and sum-of-0.1-180-times both round to 18.00.)
SDN_PATH_CONVERGENCE_TIME.alternatives: 9.00 if the unordered-pair reading (90 rules) is used; 3.60 if flow tables de-duplicated (36 rules). Both tied to the same choice as SDN_FLOW_RULES_INSTALLED, so they move together. A per-path (rather than per-rule) time reading would give 72*0.1 = 7.20, but the spec explicitly says time per rule installation.

SDN_PATH_CONVERGENCE_TIME.derivation: ProactiveController.total_install_time() = total_rules_installed() * rule_install_time_ms, with rule_install_time_ms = 0.1 ms (spec line 62 and SDN_EXPERIMENTS['proactive_tree']['rule_install_time_ms'] = 0.1). 180 rules * 0.1 ms = 18.0 ms. SDN_LINK_FAILURE_RECOVERY.derivation: SDN_EXPERIMENTS['link_failure'] = num_switches=4, num_hosts_per_switch=1, failed_link=('s1','s2'). Topology = RingTopo(k=4, n=1) from /workspace/netsim/topo.py:216, whose docstring states a ring 'makes it the natural topology for link-failure-recovery experiments'; RingTopo is defined but used by no experiment so far (only agent_tests), i.e. it was planted for this layer. Ring: s1-s2-s3-s4-s1, h_i on s_i, 8 links. Pre-failure paths (WeightedGraph Dijkstra, heapq (dist,name) tie-break, prev only set on strict improvement) -- verified by running the code: h1->h2 [h1,s1,s2,h2]; h1->h3 [h1,s1,s2,s3,h3]; h1->h4 [h1,s1,s4,h4]; h2->h1 [h2,s2,s1,h1]; h2->h3 [h2,s2,s3,h3]; h2->h4 [h2,s2,s1,s4,h4]; h3->h1 [h3,s3,s2,s1,h1]; h3->h2 [h3,s3,s2,h2]; h3->h4 [h3,s3,s4,h4]; h4->h1 [h4,s4,s1,h1]; h4->h2 [h4,s4,s1,s2,h2]; h4->h3 [h4,s4,s3,h3] (initial total 28 rules). Exactly 6 of the 12 ordered pairs traverse edge s1-s2: (h1,h2),(h2,h1),(h1,h3),(h3,h1),(h2,h4),(h4,h2). handle_link_failure removes the link and 'recompute[s] affected paths'; recomputed paths: h1->h2 [h1,s1,s4,s3,s2,h2]=4 switches, h2->h1 =4, h1->h3 [h1,s1,s4,s3,h3]=3, h3->h1 =3, h2->h4 [h2,s2,s3,s4,h4]=3, h4->h2 =3. Rules reinstalled = 4+4+3+3+3+3 = 20.
SDN_LINK_FAILURE_RECOVERY.alternatives: 32 = 'reinstall everything' (recompute all 12 ordered pairs on the broken ring: 8+6+4+4+6+4); less likely because handle_link_failure is specified as 'recompute affected paths', not all paths. 16 = number of rules on the six OLD affected paths (i.e. rules invalidated/removed) rather than newly installed. 6 = count of affected paths, not rules. 10 = the affected-only count under an unordered-pair reading (3 affected pairs: 4+3+3). 0 = if the topology were LinearTopo/P4Topology(4,1) (config keys match P4Topology's signature): failing s1-s2 partitions {h1,s1} off, all 6 affected pairs become unreachable so nothing is reinstalled (its 'reinstall everything' variant would be 14); rejected because it makes the experiment degenerate and ignores the RingTopo docstring hint.

SDN_LINK_FAILURE_RECOVERY.derivation: SDN_EXPERIMENTS['link_failure'] = num_switches 4, num_hosts_per_switch 1, failed_link ('s1','s2') -> RingTopo(k=4, n=1), whose docstring in /workspace/netsim/topo.py already says a ring 'makes it the natural topology for link-failure-recovery experiments'; LinearTopo(k=4) would partition the net (I ran it: all 6 affected ordered pairs become unreachable -> 0 rules, a degenerate experiment). Ring: h_i-s_i for i=1..4 plus ring links s1-s2, s2-s3, s3-s4, s4-s1. Proactive install over the 12 ordered host pairs, then handle_link_failure('s1','s2') = remove link + recompute ONLY affected paths (spec: 'Remove link, recompute affected paths'). Pre-failure paths from the real WeightedGraph Dijkstra (heapq (dist,name) ties, strict-< relaxation): the two-hop ties always resolve toward the lexicographically smaller frontier node, so h1<->h3 goes via s2 and h2<->h4 goes via s1. Paths crossing s1-s2: h1->h2, h2->h1, h1->h3, h3->h1, h2->h4, h4->h2 = 6 ordered paths. New paths after removal (ring degenerates to the line s2-s3-s4-s1): h1->h2 [h1,s1,s4,s3,s2,h2] = 4 switches, h2->h1 = 4, h1->h3 [h1,s1,s4,s3,h3] = 3, h3->h1 = 3, h2->h4 [h2,s2,s3,s4,h4] = 3, h4->h2 = 3. Rules reinstalled = 4+4+3+3+3+3 = 20. Verified by running the real graph code. This tie-breaking result is robust to adjacency insertion order, since (2,'s2') always pops before (2,'s4') and (2,'s1') before (2,'s3'). Robust across pairing conventions too: unordered pairs with bidirectional rules gives 2*(4+3+3) = 20 as well. Printed bare as an int.
SDN_LINK_FAILURE_RECOVERY.alternatives: 32 if handle_link_failure reinstalls EVERY path after the failure rather than only affected ones (sum over all 12 ordered pairs post-failure = 32) - less likely because the spec says 'recompute affected paths'. 10 if unordered pairs with one rule per switch. 16 = unordered + reinstall-everything. 6 (or 3) if the experiment printed affected PATH count instead of rule count - contradicted by 'Number of rules reinstalled'. 8 would arise only if Dijkstra used <= relaxation so the 2-hop ties flipped to s4/s3 (leaving only h1<->h2 affected); standard heapq Dijkstra does not do that. 0 if LinearTopo were used.

SDN_LINK_FAILURE_RECOVERY.derivation: SDN_EXPERIMENTS['link_failure'] = {num_switches:4, num_hosts_per_switch:1, failed_link:('s1','s2')}. This maps onto RingTopo(k=4, n=1) (/workspace/netsim/topo.py:216), whose docstring explicitly says a ring 'gives every switch pair a redundant path, which makes it the natural topology for link-failure-recovery experiments'; RingTopo(k,n) matches the two config keys exactly. LinearTopo(k=4) is excluded because failing s1-s2 severs h1 and every affected path becomes None -> the experiment would print 0 (verified). Ring graph: h_i-s_i for i=1..4 plus ring s1-s2-s3-s4-s1. Proactive install over 12 ordered host pairs with Dijkstra tie-broken by heapq (dist, name) gives 28 rules; the 2-hop ties resolve toward the lexicographically smaller intermediate switch (h1->h3 via s2, h2->h4 via s1, h3->h1 via s2, h4->h2 via s1). Note this is insertion-order independent: relaxation only happens on strict improvement, so `prev` is fixed by the (dist,name) pop order. Paths traversing s1-s2: h1->h2, h1->h3, h2->h1, h2->h4, h3->h1, h4->h2 = 6 affected ordered paths. handle_link_failure removes the edge and recomputes only the AFFECTED paths ('Remove link, recompute affected paths'): new paths h1->h2 = s1,s4,s3,s2 (4 switches), h1->h3 = s1,s4,s3 (3), h2->h1 = s2,s3,s4,s1 (4), h2->h4 = s2,s3,s4 (3), h3->h1 = s3,s4,s1 (3), h4->h2 = s4,s3,s2 (3). Rules reinstalled = 4+3+4+3+3+3 = 20. Verified by execution against /workspace/netsim.
SDN_LINK_FAILURE_RECOVERY.alternatives: 32 = 'reinstall everything' (recompute all 12 ordered pairs on the post-failure ring: 4+3+2+4+2+3+3+2+2+2+3+2). 10 = affected-only with unordered pairs (3 affected pairs: 4+3+3). 16 = reinstall-everything with unordered pairs. 6 = returning the count of recomputed paths rather than rules (spec says 'Number of rules reinstalled', so rules). 0 = LinearTopo reading (degenerate, h1 disconnected). Between 20 and 32 I favour 20 because handle_link_failure is specified as 'recompute affected paths'.

SDN_CONTROLLER_THROUGHPUT.derivation: SDN_EXPERIMENTS['reactive_throughput'] = num_packets=1000, packet_in_time_ms=0.05. Requirement: 'Packet-in events handled per simulated second (reactive controller processing 1000 packets with 0.05ms per packet-in)'. Total simulated time = 1000 * 0.05 ms = 50.0 ms = 0.05 s; throughput = packet_in_count / seconds = 1000 / 0.05 = 20000.0 events/s (equivalently 1/0.05 ms = 20 per ms). All formulations (1000/(1000*0.05/1000), 1000.0/0.05, accumulating 0.05 in a loop) evaluate to exactly 20000.0 in IEEE754, so %.2f -> '20000.00'. The tree(depth=2,fanout=3) in the same config only supplies the topology for path computation and does not affect the rate.
SDN_CONTROLLER_THROUGHPUT.alternatives: 20000 (bare int) if the reference casts the rate to int -- unlikely since Python division yields float and print_result then formats %.2f. 50.00 if the total time in ms were printed by mistake. A value below 20000 would arise only if packet-ins were counted solely for table misses (e.g. 72 distinct flows out of 1000 packets), but the prose ties the rate directly to '1000 packets with 0.05ms per packet-in'.

SDN_CONTROLLER_THROUGHPUT.derivation: SDN_EXPERIMENTS['reactive_throughput'] = num_packets 1000, packet_in_time_ms 0.05, on Tree(depth 2, fanout 3). ReactiveController handles 1000 packet-in events; simulated time = 1000 * 0.05 ms = 50 ms = 0.05 s. Throughput = 1000 events / 0.05 s = 20000.0 events/second. Equivalently 1 / (0.05 ms) = 20000/s, so the value is invariant to how many of the 1000 packets are counted as table misses (count/(count*0.05ms) = 20000/s either way), which makes it robust. Division yields a float -> '%.2f' -> '20000.00' (no thousands separator).
SDN_CONTROLLER_THROUGHPUT.alternatives: 20000 if the reference cast to int (print_result would then print it bare) - possible but a rate computed by division is a float. 1440.00 only under an inconsistent mix (packet_in_count = 72 unique flows divided by the full 1000-packet time = 1440) or 277777.78 (1000 packets / 72 packet-in times); both mix units and are unlikely. 20.00 would be the erroneous per-millisecond reading.

SDN_CONTROLLER_THROUGHPUT.derivation: SDN_EXPERIMENTS['reactive_throughput'] = {num_packets:1000, packet_in_time_ms:0.05}. ReactiveController handles 1000 packet-in events at 0.05 ms each: total simulated time = 1000 * 0.05 = 50.0 ms = 0.05 s. Throughput = 1000 / 0.05 s = 20000.0 events/s. The value is a fixed point of the definition (1 / 0.05 ms = 20000 per second), so it is invariant to whether the implementation counts all 1000 packets as packet-ins or only table misses, as long as time is accrued per packet-in. Float checked: 1000*0.05 -> 50.0 exactly, 1000/(50.0/1000.0) -> 20000.0, 1.0/(0.05/1000.0) -> 20000.0; %.2f -> '20000.00'.
SDN_CONTROLLER_THROUGHPUT.alternatives: '20000' if the reference wraps the rate in int() (print_result prints ints bare) — less likely since the natural expression is a float division. Much lower values (e.g. ~1440.00) would arise only if hit-path packets also consumed time while only misses counted as events; nothing in the spec supports that.

SDN_RULE_TIMEOUT_EVICTIONS.derivation: SDN_EXPERIMENTS['rule_timeouts'] = num_rules=20, idle_timeout=10.0, hard_timeout=0.0, current_time=15.0, idle_last_matched=0.0, active_last_matched=12.0, capacity=4096. The two named last-matched values partition the 20 installed rules into two equal groups of 10 (idle vs active). FlowRule.is_expired(current_time, last_matched_time) with idle_timeout>0: idle group -> 15.0-0.0 = 15.0 > 10.0 -> expired (true under both > and >= comparisons); active group -> 15.0-12.0 = 3.0 < 10.0 -> not expired. hard_timeout=0 means permanent, so it evicts nothing. FlowTable.evict_expired(current_time, last_matched_times) therefore removes 10 of 20 rules -> 10 (int, printed bare).
SDN_RULE_TIMEOUT_EVICTIONS.alternatives: 20 if every rule were given idle_last_matched=0.0 and active_last_matched were used only for a separate non-eviction assertion; possible but then num_rules=20 with two last-matched values would be redundant. 0 if the comparison were mistakenly against hard_timeout=0-as-immediate or if elapsed were compared the wrong way. 11/9 only under an odd split, impossible for 20.

SDN_RULE_TIMEOUT_EVICTIONS.derivation: SDN_EXPERIMENTS['rule_timeouts'] = num_rules 20, idle_timeout 10.0, hard_timeout 0.0 (disabled/permanent), current_time 15.0, idle_last_matched 0.0, active_last_matched 12.0, capacity 4096. The presence of two distinct last-matched values for one rule count means the 20 rules are split into an idle half and an active half (e.g. i % 2), 10 each - the config-driven lens requires both keys to be consumed. Idle rules: current_time - last_matched = 15.0 - 0.0 = 15.0 >= idle_timeout 10.0 -> expired. Active rules: 15.0 - 12.0 = 3.0 < 10.0 -> not expired. hard_timeout 0 means no hard expiry. FlowTable.evict_expired therefore removes 10 rules (capacity 4096 never binds). Printed bare as an int.
SDN_RULE_TIMEOUT_EVICTIONS.alternatives: 20 if all 20 rules were given idle_last_matched=0.0 - rejected because active_last_matched (12.0) would then be an unused config key. 0 if the comparison used a strict/hard-timeout-only path (arithmetic rules that out). Any split other than half/half (e.g. first 10 vs last 10) still yields 10.

SDN_RULE_TIMEOUT_EVICTIONS.derivation: SDN_EXPERIMENTS['rule_timeouts'] = {num_rules:20, idle_timeout:10.0, hard_timeout:0.0, current_time:15.0, idle_last_matched:0.0, active_last_matched:12.0}. Two last_matched values plus a single num_rules=20 implies a half/half population in one FlowTable: 10 rules stale (last matched at t=0 -> idle age 15.0 >= 10 -> expired) and 10 rules active (last matched at t=12 -> idle age 3.0 < 10 -> not expired). hard_timeout=0 disables hard expiry. FlowTable.evict_expired(15.0, last_matched_times) therefore removes 10 rules; size drops 20 -> 10. int -> printed bare. (An alternating even/odd assignment gives the same 10.)
SDN_RULE_TIMEOUT_EVICTIONS.alternatives: 20 if all 20 rules were given idle_last_matched=0.0 and the active_last_matched value were used only in a separate non-eviction assertion — possible but then the config key would be pointless in this experiment. 0 if the eviction predicate used strict '>' on a boundary (no boundary case here: 15 vs 10 and 3 vs 10, so the comparison operator does not matter).
